pages.x: Britain wanted to join the lands of southern Africa into one federation under its rule, and the Zulu kingdom, with its army of tens of thousands of warriors, stood in the way. In December 1878 the British high commissioner, Sir Bartle Frere, sent King Cetshwayo terms he could not accept: among them, to disband his army within a month.

Cetshwayo had ruled the Zulu since 1872 from his great royal homestead at Ulundi. He did not want war with the British, his neighbours in Natal, and told his generals to fight only on Zulu soil. When the terms ran out in January 1879, a British army under Lord Chelmsford crossed into Zululand.

On 22 January, while Chelmsford was away with half his men chasing a decoy, about 20,000 Zulu warriors fell on his camp below the hill of Isandlwana. They came on in the horns of the buffalo, a centre and two wings that closed around the camp. Within hours more than 1,300 of its defenders were dead.

That afternoon and night, some 4,000 Zulu who had missed the main battle attacked the mission station at Rorke's Drift, held by about 150 British soldiers behind walls of mealie bags and biscuit boxes. They held out until dawn, and the Zulu withdrew. Britain gave the defenders eleven Victoria Crosses.

Among the volunteers was Louis Napoléon, the exiled heir of the French emperor Napoleon III, who had trained as a British officer. On 1 June, out scouting with a small patrol, he was ambushed by Zulu warriors and killed. His death shocked Europe, and ended the best hope of the Bonapartes of ever returning to the French throne.

Chelmsford came back with a far bigger army. On 4 July 1879 he formed his men into a great hollow square on the plain before Ulundi, and the Zulu charged it again and again, into rifle volleys, cannon and Gatling guns. The charges broke before they reached the lines, and the British burned the royal homestead.

Cetshwayo fled, and was captured in the Ngome forest in August. Sir Garnet Wolseley split his kingdom among thirteen chiefs, a plan that soon led to civil war. Cetshwayo was taken to Cape Town, and in 1882 to London, where he met Queen Victoria and won much sympathy.

Isandlwana was one of the worst defeats suffered by a colonial army in the age of empire, and it is remembered with pride in South Africa. Yet the war destroyed the Zulu kingdom: within a few years it had sunk into civil war, and in 1887 Britain annexed it.
